messages.author: 7a97c986864bf6d6
messages.subject: 3d Tensor multiplication -> 3D x 3D = 2D
parts:
Hello,

I am looking for some elegant solution/function that does automated/fast tensor multiplication

3D_Matrix_1[s,k,p] x 3D_Matrix_2[p, g, k] = 2D_Matrix_3[g,s];

I can do it with some for() loop, but would be great if there was a function that speed this calculation up.

Thanks a lot.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 3d Tensor multiplication -> 3D x 3D = 2D
parts:
We don't have any tensor multiplication built in, so you'll
have to break it down into components.

Best if those are themselves matrix multiplies if possible, so the
trick's setting up the tensors to support efficient indexing. There's
a chapter in the manual on arrays vs. vectors that should help.

Overall, that loop's not going to be a big deal in terms of
efficiency, but big tensor multiplies get expensive quickly (even
multiply N x N matrices is an N^3 operation).

- Bob

Regarding speed, I'd first think about having a working implementation before even considering how fast it goes.

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 3d Tensor multiplication -> 3D x 3D = 2D
parts:
So if Einstein summation notation is what you want, and

A_skp * B_pgk -> C_sg

is what you need (multiplying and summing across k and p [I transposed your output also])

Then rearrange the B indices (call it B'):

A_skp * B'_kpg -> C_sg

Flatten the kp indices together into one new index (j) and call things matrices (Am, Bm):

Am_sj * Bm_jg -> C_sg

And that's just regular matrix multiplication I think.

Here's a little python snippet to play with:

import numpy

A = numpy.random.rand(3, 4, 5)
B = numpy.random.rand(4, 5, 3)

print numpy.einsum('ijk, jkl', A, B)

Am = A.reshape(3, 4 * 5)
Bm = B.reshape(4 * 5, 3)

print Am.dot(Bm)

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 3d Tensor multiplication -> 3D x 3D = 2D
parts:
Sure Bob,

I will try to be more specific, give the fact that I don't know much about tensor Math as well.

Tensor multiplication is useful when you have problems of deconvolution of regressions (instead of numbers), while a regression is a 2D x 2D , the sum of regressions is a tensor multiplication.

The difference in work needed between (i) using one function that takes N_dimensional tensor and is able to efficiently multiply it by a N_d or (N-1)_d,  or code it your self (in a probably dirty way), is huge.

Getting around the logic of tensor multiplication is a brain puzzle.

Thanks.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 3d Tensor multiplication -> 3D x 3D = 2D
parts:
Given a basis a 3D tensor is just a 3D array, so the we can specify
it with the N^{3} elements A_{ijk}. Then the specific operation
implied by the subjectline would be something like

C_{ij} = sum{m, n, o = 1}^{N} A_{imn} B_{jmn}

although you have to be careful about the order if the tensors are
not symmetric.

Without an efficient tensor library in Stan, however, there’s really
nothing to be gained by trying to pack a problem into tensors and
then hack tensor operations as opposed to looping over matrix
operations directly.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 3d Tensor multiplication -> 3D x 3D = 2D
parts:
Thanks---that answers my question. And it reduces the original
question to how to implement this most efficiently in Stan.
I think that's just

matrix[M, N] A[I];
matrix[M, N] B[J];

matrix[I, J] C = tensor_product(A, B);

where we define the function

// C_{ij} = sum{m, n = 1}^{N} A_{imn} B_{jmn}
matrix tensor_product(matrix[] A matrix[] B) {
matrix[size(A), size(B)] C;
for (j in 1:J)
for (i in 1:I)
c[i, j] = sum(A[i] .* B[j]);
return c;
}

I like when these things work out about as neatly as the original
formula (I removed the o variable as it wasn't used).

We could technically write analytic derivatives for sum(matrix .* matrix)
that would be both faster and less memory intensive than what you get
from the above. I turned it into an issue because I think the above
is a pain for a user to have to write if this is a common operation:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/543

- Bob
